name: mta-p3-behavior
title: Malware traffic analysis, Part 3: pivot on behavior

slides.title: Random paths, fixed rhythm: how 6 alert IPs became 15 domains.
slides.sub: I stopped following the alert IPs and followed the host's behavior instead.

slides.title: One regex found all 131 requests.
body: Each domain got its own random four-character path, like `/irpw/`.
slides.caption: Displayed: 131. 15 domains between 02:13:23 and 02:21:07 UTC.

slides.title: A new domain about every 24 seconds.
body: Inside one domain: about 2.5 s between requests. Then a 358.7 s gap before the second round.
slides.caption: www.grinswakebthu[.]info (146.59.71[.]167): seven POSTs and one GET, then the next domain.

slides.title: The GET check-in got 404 Not Found.
body: It carries an encoded `2kn1=` parameter. Most servers replied 404, with one exception (Part 4).
slides.caption: Frame 11714: GET /irpw/?2kn1=… and the 404 reply.

slides.title: After about 6 min 18 s, it started the list again.
body: Two domains were contacted twice. www.grinswakebthu[.]info had identical request sizes both times.
slides.caption: Same seven POSTs and one GET to www.grinswakebthu[.]info, at 02:14 and 02:20 UTC.

slides.title: 6 in the alerts, 9 more by behavior
bullets: The six alert IPs covered six of the 15 domains.
The other nine followed the same pattern but were not in the alerts.
All 131 requests used HTTP on port 80. No unusual ports.
The same 131 requests also had a fake User-Agent string. That one is my Dec 4 post.

slides.title: Cheat sheet: pivot from alerts to behavior
bullets: One domain's rhythm: `ip.addr == <c2 ip> && http`, plus a "Time delta from previous displayed frame" column
Same traffic, second method: `ip.src == <host> && http.user_agent contains "<string>"`
Both filters picked the same 131 requests, so the User-Agent is hardcoded in the malware.

slides.title: Part 4: what it sent, and the decoy
body: 283,087 bytes per domain visit, sent to 14 domains, and one real news site in the list.
